title: Merck-Wellcome Venture Tapped to Manufacture WHO's Top Bundibugyo Ebola Vaccine
excerpt: Hilleman Laboratories will produce clinical trial doses of IAVI's single-dose vaccine with $8.5 million in CEPI funding, as Congo's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak surpasses 3,300 cases.
body:
• Hilleman Laboratories, a Singapore-based Merck-Wellcome joint venture, will manufacture clinical trial doses of a Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI).
  • CEPI is providing up to $8.5 million in funding for the effort, as the DRC outbreak has killed 1,487 people and infected 3,360 as of July 29.
  • The WHO identified IAVI's single-dose rVSV-based vaccine as the most promising Bundibugyo candidate in May; no approved vaccine or treatment currently exists for the strain.
  • India's Serum Institute is manufacturing a rival Oxford-developed vaccine that entered its first human trial in July, while Moderna has a $50 million CEPI-backed mRNA candidate in development.

Hilleman Laboratories, a Singapore-based vaccine developer backed by pharmaceutical giant Merck and the British charity Wellcome, will manufacture doses of what the World Health Organization considers the most promising experimental vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, according to a joint announcement on Thursday.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) is providing up to $8.5 million to fund the manufacturing push, which will produce clinical-grade doses of a single-shot vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI). The vaccine uses the same recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) platform behind Merck's licensed Ervebo vaccine, which targets the more common Zaire strain of Ebola.

"With Bundibugyo virus cases rising at worrying speed, the epidemic is fast becoming a humanitarian crisis. No vaccine is currently approved against the virus, so we are urgently advancing vaccine candidates into testing."

— Richard Hatchett, CEO, CEPI

A Fast-Moving Outbreak

The urgency is driven by numbers. As of July 29, the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has infected 3,360 people and killed 1,487, according to the country's National Institute of Public Health. Confirmed cases have more than doubled since the end of June, when the count stood at 1,406, and the death toll has nearly doubled in just the past two weeks, according to Bloomberg.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola — a rarer strain that has caused only two previous outbreaks before the current epidemic. The rapid spread has overwhelmed response efforts.

"This is far faster growth than the growth in our response, and so the gap between the epidemic and our response is widening," WHO representative Mathias Harneis told reporters from Bunia, in eastern Congo. "We need to massively step up our response."

Why This Vaccine Candidate Leads

In May, the WHO singled out IAVI's rVSV-based vaccine as the most promising Bundibugyo candidate in the pipeline and recommended it be prioritized for clinical trials. The candidate was developed at the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) and has demonstrated protective efficacy in nonhuman primate studies, though it has not yet been tested in humans.

Scientists replaced the surface protein in Merck's proven Ervebo platform with one from the Bundibugyo strain, allowing them to build on technology already validated in people. IAVI received an initial $3.2 million from CEPI in June to begin generating a Master Virus Seed stock — the starting material needed to begin manufacturing. Thursday's announcement takes the next step: the actual production of clinical-grade doses by Hilleman Laboratories.

A Global Vaccine Race

IAVI's candidate is not alone. CEPI has committed up to $50 million to develop a Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine with Moderna, using its mRNA platform. Separately, CEPI invested up to $8.6 million in a vaccine from the University of Oxford built on the ChAdOx1 technology that powered the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. That candidate entered its first human trial earlier in July and is being manufactured by the Serum Institute of India.

Gavi, the global vaccine alliance, has also committed up to $40 million to support faster access and manufacturing readiness, with a preference for production capacity in Africa, according to a June statement from UNICEF and Gavi.

India's Role in the Response

Hilleman Laboratories was originally founded in India in 2009 before relocating its headquarters to Singapore in 2021. The firm operates a $20 million pilot manufacturing facility in Singapore's Biopolis research hub. Meanwhile, the Serum Institute of India — the world's largest vaccine manufacturer by volume — is playing a parallel role, producing the Oxford ChAdOx1 candidate under its existing partnership with CEPI.

Adar Poonawalla, the Serum Institute's chief executive, said in June that SII would "bring its manufacturing capabilities to this collaboration with CEPI and the University of Oxford to help advance a Bundibugyo virus vaccine candidate as quickly as possible."

What's Next

IAVI has said it expects vaccine doses to be ready for human trials by the end of 2026. If Phase 1 trials are successful, CEPI has indicated it would support late-stage trials to generate data for emergency use authorization. The race to produce and deploy a Bundibugyo vaccine is now a three-front effort spanning rVSV, mRNA, and adenoviral vector platforms — an echo of the parallel development tracks that defined the COVID-19 vaccine push.
nri_angle: India's Serum Institute is manufacturing a rival Oxford-developed Bundibugyo vaccine candidate, and Hilleman Laboratories — originally founded in India before relocating to Singapore — draws on deep ties to South Asian pharmaceutical infrastructure.
